source: Sherburne F. Cook, The Population of the California Indians, 1769-1970 (University of California Press, 1976); A. L. Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925) for the low figure of 133,000
note: The range is between scholars, not a margin of error: Kroeber's 133,000 (1925) and Cook's revised 310,000 (1976) for the eve of the Spanish missions. Some scholars think epidemics reached California before 1769, which would make both too low for 1492. In the 1833 epidemic alone at least 20,000 people died in the Central Valley (Cook, The Epidemic of 1830-1833 in California and Oregon, 1955, p. 322).

source: Benjamin Madley, An American Genocide: The United States and the California Indian Catastrophe, 1846-1873 (Yale University Press, 2016); Cook's figure for 1845
note: Madley: between 1846 and 1873 California's Native population fell from perhaps 150,000 to 30,000. Gary Clayton Anderson thinks Cook's 1845 figure may be too high.
The 1880 census counted 16,277 American Indians in California, but before 1890 the census left out Indians it did not tax, so the count is too low to compare.

label: 1.9–7+ million
source: Douglas H. Ubelaker, North American Indian population size, A.D. 1500 to 1985, American Journal of Physical Anthropology 77 (1988): 289-294 (1,894,350); Russell Thornton, American Indian Holocaust and Survival (University of Oklahoma Press, 1987) (7+ million, over 5 million in the present-day United States), both as reported in National Research Council, America Becoming, vol. 1 (2001), ch. 5
note: North of Mexico, about 1500. The estimates differ by method: Ubelaker adds up tribe-by-tribe figures; Thornton allows for epidemics before any written count.

source: Russell Thornton, American Indian Holocaust and Survival (1987), as cited in J. David Hacker and Michael R. Haines, American Indian Mortality in the Late Nineteenth Century, NBER Working Paper 12572 (2006)
